newsitem.title: USA: Wall Street bets Fed will keep interest rates steady.
newsitem.headline: Wall Street bets Fed will keep interest rates steady.

text.p: The stock market is betting the Federal Reserve will hold the line on interest rates even though economic data might argue for a cut, but some experts believe a reduction would be like waving a red flag in front of an already charging bull.
This week, investors wrote obituaries about inflation, which has been dead for years, as the stock market repeated its high-wire act.

The Dow Jones industrial average moved closer to the 7,000-point level, powered by good news on inflation as it gained 116.61 points for the week, ending Friday at 6,813.09, down 10.77 points for the day.

The market turned to next week's meeting of the central bank's policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee. But unlike the past year, there was no evidence of the usual paranoia leading up to the FOMC's meeting.
Investors were not worried that at the meeting Feb. 4 and 5 the Fed would raise interest rates, which could threaten to bring down the longest bull market in history.

In fact, there was jubilation in some quarters that based on the current economic numbers that showed inflation was still in check, perhaps later this year, the Fed might actually reduce interest rates.
The inflation barometers released this week helped soothe investors' jitters.
The Employment Cost Index rose 0.8 percent in the fourth quarter, up from the 0.6 percent rise in the third quarter, but within the comfort zone of inflation-wary investors.

In a report on the nation's gross domestic product for the last three months of 1996, the implicit price deflator, a broad measure of inflation, rose at a 1.4 percent annual rate in the fourth quarter, down from 1.7 percent in the third quarter.

The Fed's biggest worry is that inflation might flare up with the economy in its sixth year of expansion. Over the years, the Fed has raised interest rates to halt inflation until the boom turned to bust.

But now that inflation -- as measured last year by the Consumer Price Index and Producer Price Index -- stands at the lowest levels in decades, some analysts believe the Fed should consider a rate cut.
But don't hold your breath, they say, because the central bank has added another factor to its monetary decision making -- the exuberant stock market.

Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan is uncomfortable with what looks like a runaway stock market and anything that would increase the enthusiasm of investors is something that he would prefer to avoid at this time.
"We believe that the Fed should drop short-term interest rates now," says Don Hays, director of investment strategy at Wheat First Butcher Singer in Richmond, Va.
"But it is obvious that 'irrational exuberance' has clouded Mr. Greenspan's vision," he said.

In December, Greenspan rattled the stock market with a comment warning of "irrational exuberance" in financial markets, fuelling speculation the central bank might hike interest rates to cool things down.

Hays said that in the past, Wall Street has been able to get a good idea about the Fed's next monetary move simply by tracking the performance of bonds, the dollar and the price of a basket of industrial commodities and gold.
The way the so-called "Three Vigilantes" are now behaving should send a wakeup call for the central bank to cut rates, Hays said.
Vigilante No. 1 -- Treasury bond yields have fallen recently, which points to a slowing economy and subdued inflation.
The jump this week in the dollar to a four-year high against the Japanese yen suggested that currency traders were being drawn by the high U.S. interest rates, and it might be time to lower them.
Perhaps the most striking is the plunge in gold -- a prime barometer of inflation -- to less than $350 an ounce and its lowest level in more than three years this week.
"So what's the excuse Mr. Greenspan?," Hays asked. "It is now his new vigilante -- irrational exuberance."
He reckoned that the Fed chief's "desire" to control exuberance in financial markets will delay any cut in interest rates.
Wall Street has ruled out the chance that the Fed could raise interest rates because the economy is still behaving.
Also international factors are affecting Fed policy, and a boost in interest rates would further weaken the depressed Japanese yen, which could precipitate a serious banking crisis in Japan.

The big concern this year is the tight labour market and the possible impact that it might have on wages. With the economy in its sixth year of expansion and unemployment at just 5.3 percent, there's a risk of rising labour costs.

"Eventually the Fed is more likely to lower interest rates since there's little inflation, but a cut may only come in six to 12 months," said Dave Ranson director of research at H.C. Wainwright & Co. in Boston.

"Greenspan made a comment a week ago about the employment rate being so low at 5.3 percent but the concern is based on an old fallacy that has been believed for decades by economists that a low unemployment rate is a threat to inflation," he said. "Economists who still believe that theory are working with old economic models of the 1930s."
Ranson said that the rate of unemployment has not had any significant impact over the past 30 years in driving up future inflation.
"Low unemployment is a sign of how the economy is performing and low unemployment is a sign of great success," he said.
On Friday, the Nasdaq Composite index up 8.83 points to 1,379.85. The index was up 16.03 on the week.

The Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks rose 1.99 to 786.16, leaving that index 15.64 points higher for the week. The American Stock Exchange index edged up 0.11 to 588.77, and gained 0.61 on the week.
